title: Your local shrine
hook: a shrine may be closer than you think

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lourdes and Fatima as pilgrims, where wheelchairs lead the procession and volunteers push. Your line was the sick go first. Who did you offer a ride, or a slower walk? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

Forty minutes up the highway, past a gas station and a feed store, there's a turnoff with a small brown sign. A gravel road. A grotto made of fieldstone, with a statue of Mary in it and rows of candles in red glass. A rack of rosaries left by people who prayed and went home. A plaque from the parish that built it. On a weekday afternoon there's a retired couple on a bench, a man in work boots kneeling on the gravel, and a woman reading the handwritten notes tucked into the stones. None of them flew anywhere. Some of them drove past this sign for years before they ever stopped. Today, the shrine near you.
screen: `A SMALL BROWN SIGN OFF THE HIGHWAY.` → `A GROTTO OF FIELDSTONE.` → `NOBODY FLEW ANYWHERE.`

segments.voice: First, what a shrine is. The Church's Code of Canon Law defines one simply: a church or other sacred place that the faithful visit on pilgrimage for a particular reason of devotion, with the approval of the local bishop. So a shrine is not measured by size or fame. It's measured by prayer: people come there on purpose. Second, the oldest pattern. In Genesis, Jacob is running from his brother. He stops for the night at an ordinary spot, puts a stone under his head, and dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven. He wakes up and says, in effect, the Lord was in this place and I didn't know it. Then he sets the stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. Moments before, he had called it the house of God. He didn't travel to a famous holy site. He found one on the road he was already on. Third, why local shrines matter. A grand pilgrimage may come once in a lifetime, and some people can never make one: too sick, too poor, too busy caring for someone. A shrine within driving distance, or a bus ride away, is a pilgrimage for the rest of us. It can hold a grandparent's devotion, a parish's history, an immigrant community's patron saint, brought from home. Last, how to find one. Your diocese's website or the parish office can tell you which shrines are near. Some sit beside a big church. Some are a single statue at the edge of a cemetery. The pilgrimage can be an afternoon. The prayer can be the same.
screen: `A PLACE PEOPLE VISIT TO PRAY.` · `JACOB'S STONE PILLOW AT BETHEL.` · `A PILGRIMAGE FOR THE REST OF US.` · `ASK THE PARISH OR THE DIOCESE.` · then, large: `THE LORD WAS IN THIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your nearest shrine. You can look after the bell; for now, prepare. Settle, and breathe. Think of places within an hour of you where people go to pray. A grotto. A statue at a crossroads. A chapel you've driven past. A side altar with candles always lit. Which one comes to mind? Picture yourself pulling off the road and walking in. What would you bring? A name, a worry, a thank-you. If you pray, you can offer that intention now and promise to bring it in person. If you don't, just choose the place. The bell holds the time.
Your local shrine. A church or sacred place near you that people visit on pilgrimage, with the bishop's approval. A pilgrimage in an afternoon. Today's word.
Your line: close to home. Today, look up the nearest shrine, and put a date on your calendar to visit it. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics visit diocesan and national shrines near home for a day of prayer, Mass and confession; dioceses and parishes list approved shrines and sometimes organize local pilgrimages to them.

original.note: Latin: the word the Code of Canon Law uses for a shrine.

trapdoor: what you thought: shrines are famous places far away.
what it means: any church or sacred place people visit on pilgrimage, with the bishop's approval; often one is close to home.
what a scholar hears: canon 1230 defines a shrine by pilgrimage and the local ordinary's approval, not by fame.

notes: Index hook 'most dioceses have a shrine within reach' is a count claim; the teaser hook and script avoid it.

Canon 1230 paraphrased: a church or other sacred place to which the faithful make pilgrimage for a special reason of piety, with the approval of the local ordinary. Confirm, and confirm the Latin term 'sanctuarium'.

Genesis 28 paraphrased (Jacob's words are given 'in effect', not quoted). 'Bethel, house of God': Genesis 28:19 names the place Bethel; the meaning 'house of God' is from Jacob's words in 28:17. Confirm.
Most-claims avoided; 'a grand pilgrimage may come once in a lifetime' is hedged; confirm.
The hook's grotto is an invented composite scene, not a named shrine.

Editor: 'Bethel, house of God' read as an etymology; now the script says only what Genesis 28:17–19 says (Jacob calls the place the house of God, then names it Bethel), in the teach, the match pair and the fork reveal.
